subject: Very different optimizing results for centered vs non centered parameterisation

messages.author: ee490f1373633c05
messages.subject: Very different optimizing results for centered vs non centered parameterisation
parts:
Hello!

I am running a large vector autoregression model with a t distribution on the coefficients to help variable selection.

If I understand correctly, the centered parameterisation and non-centered parameterisation give different modes (because the integral of the density function is the same between equivalent points but not the density function itself).

Sampling is quite slow due to the large size of the model, so I thought I would give optimisation a try. (Meanfield ADVI does not converge in a reasonable number of iterations and full rank ADVI doesn't work at all).

With the non-centered parameterisation, which I use for sampling, the outputs are nothing like with sampling, including predictive performance. When I use the centered parameterisation, the model parameters are much closer to the sampling outputs, and the predictive performance of the model is much more similar.

Is this expected behaviour?

Quite interesting...

Julian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Very different optimizing results for centered vs non centered parameterisation
parts:
Do you have an example? And do the centered and non-centered
parameterizations produce roughly the same posteriors for the
quantities of interest?

Optimization drops any Jacobians due to constraints. I wrote
up a little case study:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html

But it's hard to say more without the code and example data.

And by nothing like, I take it you're comparing posterior modes
to posterior means? Those aren't necessarily going to be anywhere
near each other (I have another case study explaining this in
the works).

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Very different optimizing results for centered vs non centered parameterisation
parts: Because sampling targets a conditional measure and optimization targets a conditional density.  They are fundamentally different objects and transform in different ways.  In particular, a MAP is not defined for a measure but rather a density in a specific parameterization, which is why we don't want to include Jacobians that change this density when we do temporary transformations behind the scenes.

On Sep 20, 2016, at 23:01, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Not that I know of, but it probably wouldn't be hard to support
a MAP option that leaves the Jacobians in by default.

For now, you'd have to use unconstrained variables and write your
own Jacobian into the model directly.  Or use an external optimizer
on the log_prob function from R.

- Bob

Hi Julian,

   The high correlation among the parameters in the posterior distribution could cause high autocorrelation among the MCMC sampling. In some cases, centered parameterisation could reduce the correlations. I think this might be the case in your work. Maybe you will find this paper to be helpful:
https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~scs/Courses/Stat376/Papers/GelfandBiometrika1995.pdf.

Best,

Lu Zhang
